cpss1996.title: Settlement Risk in Foreign Exchange Transactions
cpss1996.author: Committee on Payment and Settlement Systems of the central banks of the Group of Ten countries; Steering Group chaired by Peter W. Allsopp (the Allsopp Report)
cpss1996.quote: In the absence of a settlement arrangement that ensures that the final transfer of one currency will occur if and only if the final transfer of the other currency also occurs, one party to an FX trade could pay out the currency it sold but not receive the currency it bought.
supports: Title page as printed: 'BANK FOR INTERNATIONAL SETTLEMENTS / SETTLEMENT RISK IN FOREIGN EXCHANGE TRANSACTIONS / Report prepared by the Committee on Payment and Settlement Systems of the central banks of the Group of Ten countries / Basle / March 1996'. Venue check: the PDF says Basle, March 1996, CPSS report (later indexed as CPMI Papers no 17).
Chairman of the Steering Group, verbatim from the members list: 'Mr. Peter W. Allsopp, Chairman' / 'Bank of England'.

Foreword, verbatim: 'The Committee on Payment and Settlement Systems is indebted to Peter Allsopp for his excellent leadership in chairing the Steering Group. Mr. Allsopp, who has made many fine contributions to the work of the Committee and its predecessor over the years, is retiring from the Bank of England this year.'

Section 2.2.1, verbatim: 'On 26th June 1974 the Bundesaufsichtsamt fur das Kreditwesen withdrew the banking licence of Bankhaus Herstatt, a small bank in Cologne active in the FX market, and ordered it into liquidation during the banking day but after the close of the interbank payments system in Germany.'

Section 2.2.1, verbatim: 'Upon the termination of Herstatt's business at 10.30 a.m. New York time on 26th June (3.30 p.m. in Frankfurt), Herstatt's New York correspondent bank suspended outgoing US dollar payments from Herstatt's account.'

Section 2.1, verbatim: 'It is also referred to as Herstatt risk, although this is an inappropriate term given the differing circumstances, including those described below, in which this risk has materialised.'

Glossary, verbatim: 'Payment versus payment (PVP): a mechanism in a foreign exchange settlement system that ensures that a final transfer of one currency occurs if and only if a final transfer of the other currency or currencies takes place.'

Nickname check: 'the Allsopp Report' is NOT printed anywhere in the 1996 PDF. It is attested in a later BIS/CPSS report - CPSS, 'Progress in reducing foreign exchange settlement risk', May 2008 (CPMI Papers no 83), PDF p 22: 'The 1996 report on Settlement risks in foreign exchange transactions (the Allsopp Report) therefore laid down a three-track strategy to reduce the systemic risks associated with FX settlements'. The 1996 report itself uses the same naming convention for its predecessors (the Angell, Lamfalussy and Noel Reports).

galati2002.title: Settlement risk in foreign exchange markets and CLS Bank
galati2002.author: Gabriele Galati
galati2002.quote: On 26 June 1974, at 15:30 CET, the German authorities closed Bankhaus Herstatt, a medium-sized bank that was very active in foreign exchange markets.
supports: Venue as printed in the PDF footer: 'BIS Quarterly Review, December 2002', pages 55-65.

Footnote 3, verbatim: 'The value of transactions to be settled for Bankhaus Herstatt was estimated at $200 million. Some banks had also entered into forward trades with Herstatt. These trades were not yet due to be settled when the bank was closed and had to be replaced.'
Verbatim: 'Herstatt's closure started a chain reaction that disrupted payment and settlement systems. Its New York correspondent bank suspended all US dollar payments from the German bank's account.'

Verbatim: 'Other banks in New York refused to make payments on their own account or for their customers until they received confirmation that their countervalue had been received. These disruptions were propagated further through the multilateral net settlement system used in New York. Over the next three days, the amount of gross funds transferred by this system declined by an estimated 60%.'

Verbatim: 'In September 2002, CLS Bank went into operation, settling transactions involving seven currencies: the US dollar, euro, yen, pound sterling, Swiss franc, Canadian dollar and Australian dollar.'

Verbatim: 'Payments to CLS Bank are executed between 07:00 and 12:00 CET, subject to strict hourly deadlines. At least part of this time is within the operating hours of six of the seven RTGS systems used to make payments to and from CLS Bank.'
Verbatim: 'at 06:30 CET issues a pay-in schedule for each member.'
Verbatim, the limit on the window claim: 'In Australia, CLS payments are made during a special evening session of the payment system.'

bech2019.title: FX settlement risk remains significant
bech2019.author: Morten Linnemann Bech and Henry Holden
bech2019.quote: At 15:30 CET on 26 June 1974, the German authorities closed the bank down.
supports: Venue as printed on the page: 'BIS Quarterly Review | December 2019 | 08 December 2019'.
Verbatim: 'While Herstatt had already received Deutsche marks from its counterparties, it had not yet made the corresponding US dollar payments in New York.'

Verbatim: 'Herstatt's failure to pay led banks more generally to stop outgoing payments until they were sure their countervalues had been received. The international payment system then froze, and the erosion of trust caused lending rates to spike and credit to be curtailed.'
Verbatim: 'This left an estimated $8.9 trillion worth of FX payments at risk on any given day.'
Verbatim: 'in 2002 market participants set up Continuous Linked Settlement (CLS), a specialist institution that settles FX transactions on a payment-versus-payment (PvP) basis.'

glowka2022.title: FX settlement risk: an unsettled issue
glowka2022.author: Marc Glowka and Thomas Nilsson
glowka2022.quote: In April 2022, $2.2 trillion of daily FX turnover was subject to settlement risk, up from an estimated $1.9 trillion in April 2019.
supports: Venue as printed in the PDF footer: 'BIS Quarterly Review, December 2022', page 75 onward.
Verbatim: 'Of this, $2.5 trillion was settled via CLS, a global financial market infrastructure that provides for PvP in 18 currencies (see CPSS (2008), Annex 4, for details on CLS).'
Verbatim: 'The remaining $2.2 trillion was settled via on-us without loss protection or via other non-PvP arrangements and is therefore subject to risk.'
Verbatim: 'For example, a PvP arrangement may not operate within a time window that matches periods of peak liquidity.'

bcbshistory.title: History of the Basel Committee
bcbshistory.author: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision / Bank for International Settlements
bcbshistory.quote: The Basel Committee - initially named the Committee on Banking Regulations and Supervisory Practices - was established by the central bank Governors of the Group of Ten countries at the end of 1974 in the aftermath of serious disturbances in international currency and banking markets (notably the failure of Bankhaus Herstatt in West Germany).
supports: Verbatim: 'The Committee's first meeting took place in February 1975, and meetings have been held regularly three or four times a year since.'
Page metadata: <meta name='DC.date' content='2014-10-09'>.

unverified: That 07:00-12:00 CET is the only stretch when CLS's national payment systems are all open at once - Galati 2002 says only that 'at least part of this time is within the operating hours of six of the seven RTGS systems used to make payments to and from CLS Bank', and that 'in Australia, CLS payments are made during a special evening session of the payment system'. The prose now claims only the six-of-seven overlap; the 'all open' gloss is removed from the story and from card p2c01-c5.

Whether Herstatt was a small or a medium-sized bank - CPSS 1996 section 2.2.1 says 'a small bank in Cologne active in the FX market', while Galati 2002 and Bech and Holden 2019 both say 'medium-sized'. No size adjective is used in the prose or on a card.

The widely repeated figure that Herstatt's collapse cost banks 'some $620 million' - it appears in trade press (American Banker) but not in any BIS source I opened; BIS (Galati 2002, footnote 3) instead estimates the transactions awaiting settlement at $200 million, and that is the number used in the prose.
Iwan D. Herstatt's own conduct, role or intentions in June 1974 - no primary source opened, so he is not named in the prose or on a card.

Whether CLS still covers exactly 18 currencies in 2026, and the 2025 Triennial Survey's at-risk figure - the most recent BIS article opened is the December 2022 Quarterly Review, so the prose is stated as of April 2022.

That the German regulator's action was at 16:30 CET, as the allocation note stated - two BIS sources (Galati 2002 and Bech and Holden 2019) both say 15:30 CET, and CPSS 1996 says '3.30 p.m. in Frankfurt'. 15:30 is used.
